claim: Animal African trypanosomosis (AAT) puts upward of a million head of livestock at risk across 37 countries in Africa.
source: Animal African trypanosomosis (AAT), caused by protist parasites of the genus Trypanosoma, puts upward of a million head of livestock at risk across 37 countries in Africa.
evidence: This is a statement about the geographic scope and scale of AAT risk, presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: AAT is caused by protist parasites of the genus Trypanosoma.
source: Animal African trypanosomosis (AAT), caused by protist parasites of the genus Trypanosoma, puts upward of a million head of livestock at risk across 37 countries in Africa.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the causative agent of AAT, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: The SHERLOCK4AAT toolbox includes Pan-trypanosomatid, Trypanozoon, T. vivax, T. congolense, T. theileri, T. simiae, and T. suis assays.
source: We have adapted the CRISPR-based detection toolkit SHERLOCK (Specific High-sensitivity Enzymatic Reporter unLOCKing) for trypanosomatid parasites responsible for AAT (SHERLOCK4AAT) including Pan-trypanosomatid, Trypanozoon, T. vivax, T. congolense, T. theileri, T. simiae, and T. suis assays.
evidence: This describes the specific assays developed in this study, representing data from the research.

claim: 62.7% [58.1, 67.3] of pigs were found infected with at least one trypanosome species.
source: 62.7% [58.1, 67.3] of pigs were found infected with at least one trypanosome species.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study with confidence intervals, representing experimental data.

claim: T. brucei gambiense was found in one animal at both sites.
source: T. brucei gambiense, a human-infectious trypanosome, was found in one animal at both sites, highlighting the risk that these animals may act as persistent reservoirs.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's screening results.

claim: T. brucei gambiense is a human-infectious trypanosome.
source: T. brucei gambiense, a human-infectious trypanosome, was found in one animal at both sites, highlighting the risk that these animals may act as persistent reservoirs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the pathogenicity of T. brucei gambiense.

claim: Pigs could act as sentinels to monitor T. b. gambiense circulation using the SHERLOCK4AAT toolbox.
source: These data suggest that, due to their proximity to humans and their attractiveness to tsetse flies, pigs could act as sentinels to monitor T. b. gambiense circulation using the SHERLOCK4AAT toolbox.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings and reasoning about pig characteristics.

claim: Reported annual cases of gambiense HAT have been maintained below 1000 since 2018.
source: Reported annual cases have been maintained below 1000 since 2018, making the elimination (zero transmission) of gambiense HAT (gHAT) by 2030, one of the major objectives of the World Health Organisation (WHO), achievable (Franco et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Franco et al., 2024.

claim: Elimination of gambiense HAT by 2030 is one of the major objectives of the WHO.
source: Reported annual cases have been maintained below 1000 since 2018, making the elimination (zero transmission) of gambiense HAT (gHAT) by 2030, one of the major objectives of the World Health Organisation (WHO), achievable (Franco et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Franco et al., 2024.

claim: AAT represents a threat to livestock and smallholder economies.
source: Nevertheless, animal African trypanosomosis (AAT), also known as nagana, remains a significant burden to sustainable agricultural development, and represents a threat to livestock and smallholder economies (Boulangé et al., 2022), with a total estimated loss of 4.75 billion USD per year in terms of agricultural gross domestic product in tsetse-infested lands (Budd, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boulangé et al., 2022.

claim: AAT causes a total estimated loss of 4.75 billion USD per year in terms of agricultural gross domestic product in tsetse-infested lands.
source: Nevertheless, animal African trypanosomosis (AAT), also known as nagana, remains a significant burden to sustainable agricultural development, and represents a threat to livestock and smallholder economies (Boulangé et al., 2022), with a total estimated loss of 4.75 billion USD per year in terms of agricultural gross domestic product in tsetse-infested lands (Budd, 2001).
evidence: This economic estimate is supported by citation to Budd, 2001.

claim: HAT is caused by either Trypanosoma brucei gambiense in West Africa, or T. b. rhodesiense in East Africa.
source: Unlike HAT, which is caused by either Trypanosoma brucei (T. b.) gambiense in West Africa, or T. b. rhodesiense in East Africa, AAT encompasses a wider range of trypanosomatid parasites.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the causative agents and geographic distribution of HAT.

claim: Animal-infecting trypanosomes including T. vivax, T. congolense, T. brucei, T. theileri, T. simiae, and T. suis are transmitted by blood-sucking flies in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: In sub-Saharan Africa, animal-infecting trypanosomes including T. vivax, T. congolense, T. brucei, T. theileri, T. simiae, and T. suis are transmitted by blood-sucking flies, such as Glossinidae and Tabanidae, to a wide range of wild and domestic mammals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome transmission.

claim: Socio-environmental factors such as land cover, humidity, temperature, and livestock migration impact trypanosome transmission.
source: Socio-environmental factors such as land cover, humidity, temperature, and livestock migration impact trypanosome transmission (Karshima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Karshima et al., 2016.

claim: Symptoms of AAT are host and pathogen-dependent.
source: Symptoms of AAT are host and pathogen-dependent, with an infection potentially leading to spontaneous abortions, reduction in milk and meat production, delays in sexual maturity, low calving rates, loss of draught power, and ultimately to high mortality, all of which compound poverty in many sub-Saharan countries (Kristjanson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kristjanson et al., 1999.

claim: Microscopy-based methods lack sensitivity with a limit of detection ranging from 104 to 105 parasites/ml when using fresh blood.
source: Microscopy-based methods are the most commonly used diagnostic methods, but lack sensitivity with a limit of detection (LoD) ranging from 104 to 105 parasites/ml when using fresh blood, to 250–5000 parasites/ml for methods combining centrifugation (Desquesnes et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Desquesnes et al., 2022a.

claim: Molecular diagnostic techniques including PCR and LAMP offer increased sensitivity (73–100%) and LoD (1–1000 parasites/ml).
source: In contrast, molecular diagnostic techniques, including PCR and Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), offer increased sensitivity (73–100%) and LoD (1–1000 parasites/ml) by targeting specific regions of the parasites' DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about molecular diagnostic performance.

claim: Domestic animals such as pigs, dogs, cattle, sheep, and goats are suspected reservoirs of T. b. gambiense.
source: AAT-related trypanosome species circulate co-endemically with T. b. gambiense in West and Central Africa, where domestic animals such as pigs, dogs, cattle, sheep, and goats are suspected reservoirs (Magang et al., 2023; Traoré et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Magang et al., 2023 and Traoré et al., 2021.

claim: Free-range pigs in a historical HAT focus in Côte d'Ivoire were identified as reservoirs for T. b. gambiense.
source: In a historical HAT focus in Côte d'Ivoire, free-range pigs sharing the same environment as humans were identified as reservoirs for T. b. gambiense (Traoré et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Traoré et al., 2021.

claim: The diagnostic techniques employed in the Côte d'Ivoire study tended to overestimate the prevalence of human infective parasites in pigs.
source: The diagnostic techniques employed in this study, involving single round (Radwanska et al., 2002) or nested PCR (Morrison et al., 2008), however, tended to overestimate the prevalence of the human infective parasites in pigs (Traoré et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to Radwanska et al., 2002, Morrison et al., 2008, and Traoré et al., 2021.

claim: SHERLOCK offers unprecedented levels of diagnostic specificity and sensitivity.
source: For this purpose, we have adapted the Specific High-sensitivity Enzymatic Reporter unLOCKing (SHERLOCK) detection that offers unprecedented levels of diagnostic specificity and sensitivity (Gootenberg et al., 2017), and has been adapted for the detection of HAT (Sima et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gootenberg et al., 2017 and Sima et al., 2022.

claim: SHERLOCK combines isothermal amplification by recombinase polymerase with Cas13a detection of the target RNA.
source: SHERLOCK combines an isothermal amplification by recombinase polymerase (RPA) with Cas13a detection of the target RNA (Gootenberg et al., 2017; Kellner et al., 2019; Piepenburg et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gootenberg et al., 2017, Kellner et al., 2019, and Piepenburg et al., 2006.

claim: A total of 424 blood samples were collected from two populations of domestic pigs.
source: A total of 424 blood samples were collected (1) from free-ranging pigs in the last hypo-endemic foci of gHAT in Côte d'Ivoire, and (2) from farm pigs bred in the historical gHAT focus of forested Guinea where unconfirmed seropositive cases of gHAT are still sporadically detected (Courtin et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the sample collection in the study.

claim: The 18S rRNA gene shares over 70% identity between Kinetoplastea members.
source: In addition to being a multicopy gene, the 18S rRNA gene shares over 70% identity between Kinetoplastea members (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The region between 1535–1672 bp of the 18S rRNA gene was found to be conserved between all trypanosomatid species.
source: Using BLAST analysis, the region between 1535–1672 bp (XR_002989632.1) was found to be conserved between all trypanosomatid species and was selected as the pan-trypanosomatid SHERLOCK target.
evidence: This is a finding from BLAST analysis performed in the study.

claim: SHERLOCK has the capacity to discriminate between two sequences differing by a single nucleotide.
source: SHERLOCK has the capacity to discriminate between two sequences differing by a single nucleotide (Gootenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gootenberg et al., 2017.

claim: The pan-Trypanozoon SHERLOCK assay can discriminate between species belonging to the Trypanozoon subgenus from other non-Trypanozoon trypanosomes.
source: The pan-Trypanozoon SHERLOCK assay can discriminate between the species belonging to the Trypanozoon subgenus (T. b. spp., T. evansi types A and B, and T. equiperdum) from other non-Trypanozoon trypanosomes or other co-endemic parasites.
evidence: This describes the specificity of the assay based on the design and validation.

claim: The IFX gene has no apparent homologue in any other Trypanosoma species or other related parasites.
source: The invariant flagellum antigen (IFX) gene has no apparent homologue in any other Trypanosoma species or other related parasites, and was therefore selected (Autheman et al., 2021; Romero-Ramirez et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Autheman et al., 2021 and Romero-Ramirez et al., 2022.

claim: The single pan-trypanosomatid assay detected RNA from all trypanosomatid species tested but not from HEK cells or Plasmodium falciparum.
source: The single pan-trypanosomatid assay detected RNA from all trypanosomatid species tested (T. b. brucei, T. b. gambiense, T. b. rhodesiense, T. evansi (type A and B), T. equiperdum, T. congolense, T. vivax, T. theileri, T. cruzi, and Leishmania major) but not from HEK cells, synthetic controls for T. simiae and T. suis or co-endemic parasites such as Plasmodium falciparum (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The pan-Trypanozoon assay detected only RNA from members of the Trypanozoon subgenus.
source: The pan-Trypanozoon assay detected only RNA from members of the Trypanozoon subgenus (T. b. brucei, T. b. gambiense, T. b. rhodesiense, T. evansi (type A and B), and T. equiperdum) but not from HEK cells, synthetic controls for T. simiae and T. suis or co-endemic parasites such as T. congolense, T. vivax, T. theileri, and P. falciparum (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The species-specific T. congolense, T. vivax, T. theileri, T. simiae, and T. suis assays only detected their respective targeted parasite RNA with no cross-reactivity.
source: The species-specific T. congolense, T. vivax, T. theileri, T. simiae, and T. suis assays only detected their respective targeted parasite RNA or synthetic controls with no cross-reactivity with any other RNAs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For the single pan-trypanosomatid assay, the LoD was between 10 and 103 parasites per ml.
source: For the single pan-trypanosomatid assay, the LoD was between 10 and 103 parasites per ml.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from LoD experiments.

claim: The pan-Trypanozoon and T. theileri assays tested 10 parasites per ml.
source: The pan-Trypanozoon and T. theileri assays tested 10 parasites per ml.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from LoD experiments.

claim: For the T. congolense assay, the LoD was found between 10 and 103 parasites per mL.
source: For the T. congolense assay, the LoD was found between 10 and 103 parasites per mL, and between 104 and 105 parasites per ml for the T. vivax test (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For the T. vivax test, the LoD was between 104 and 105 parasites per ml.
source: For the T. congolense assay, the LoD was found between 10 and 103 parasites per mL, and between 104 and 105 parasites per ml for the T. vivax test (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: T. simiae and T. suis tests showed an LoD between 10 and 100 fM.
source: The sensitivity of T. simiae and T. suis tests was evaluated on synthetic positive controls, as no genetic materials were available, and both showed an LoD between 10 and 100 fM (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Multiplexing crRNAs increased the median sensitivity from 66.1% to 74.7%.
source: Multiplexing crRNAs increased the median sensitivity from 66.1% to 74.7%, while keeping specificity above 80% (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The positivity threshold value for the pan-trypanosomatid test was 6.050.
source: The positivity threshold values were 6.050 for the pan-trypanosomatid test, 11.70 for the pan-Trypanozoon test, 1.923 for the T. congolense test, 1.831 for the T. vivax test, 1.805 for the T. theileri test, 1.546 for the T. simiae test, and 2.609 for the T. suis test (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Côte d'Ivoire, blood samples were collected from 224 free-ranging pigs.
source: In Côte d'Ivoire, blood samples were collected from 224 free-ranging pigs across the rural districts of Bonon, Bouaflé, Sinfra, Vavoua, and Brobo (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology.

claim: In the N'zérékoré prefecture of Forested Guinea, 200 farm pigs were sampled.
source: In the N'zérékoré prefecture of Forested Guinea, 200 farm pigs were sampled, with a focus on organized farming communities (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology.

claim: 74.6% [68.9, 80.3] (167/224) of the samples tested positive in at least one SHERLOCK assay in Côte d'Ivoire.
source: In total, 74.6% [68.9, 80.3] (167/224) of the samples tested positive in at least one SHERLOCK assay in Côte d'Ivoire (Figure 4B), and 49.5% [42.6, 56.9] (99/200) in Guinea (Figure 5B) representing a high apparent prevalence of trypanosome infections in these two populations of pigs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the screening with confidence intervals, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 49.5% [42.6, 56.9] (99/200) of samples tested positive in at least one SHERLOCK assay in Guinea.
source: In total, 74.6% [68.9, 80.3] (167/224) of the samples tested positive in at least one SHERLOCK assay in Côte d'Ivoire (Figure 4B), and 49.5% [42.6, 56.9] (99/200) in Guinea (Figure 5B) representing a high apparent prevalence of trypanosome infections in these two populations of pigs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the screening with confidence intervals, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 47.3% [40.8, 53.8] (106/224) of the pigs from Côte d'Ivoire tested positive using at least one parasitological method.
source: In parallel, 47.3% [40.8, 53.8] (106/224) of the pigs from Côte d'Ivoire tested positive using at least one parasitological method (buffy coat examination, mAECT and/or isolation in mice; results detailed in a separate study, manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from parasitological testing with confidence intervals.

claim: The combination of SHERLOCK4AAT assays may compete with combined parasitological methods in terms of sensitivity (median sensitivity 91.4% vs 84.3%).
source: This analysis suggested that, in terms of sensitivity, the combination of SHERLOCK4AAT assays may compete with combined parasitological methods (i.e., median sensitivity 91.4% vs 84.3%) while controlling median specificity above 75% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 41.1% [34.6, 47.6] of the samples from Côte d'Ivoire (90/219) were positive using the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid assay.
source: Using the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid assay, 41.1% [34.6, 47.6] of the samples from Côte d'Ivoire (90/219) and 29.5% [23.2, 35.8] from Guinea (59/200) were positive (Figures 4C and 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with confidence intervals, shown in Figures 4C and 5C.

claim: 29.5% [23.2, 35.8] of samples from Guinea (59/200) were positive using the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid assay.
source: Using the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid assay, 41.1% [34.6, 47.6] of the samples from Côte d'Ivoire (90/219) and 29.5% [23.2, 35.8] from Guinea (59/200) were positive (Figures 4C and 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with confidence intervals, shown in Figures 4C and 5C.

claim: The pan-Trypanozoon assay identified 38.0% [31.6, 44.4] (85/224) of samples in Côte d'Ivoire.
source: The pan-Trypanozoon assay identified 38.0% [31.6, 44.4] (85/224) and 39.0% [32.2, 45.8] (78/200) of samples in each country, respectively (Figures 4C and 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with confidence intervals, shown in Figures 4C and 5C.

claim: The pan-Trypanozoon assay identified 39.0% [32.2, 45.8] (78/200) of samples in Guinea.
source: The pan-Trypanozoon assay identified 38.0% [31.6, 44.4] (85/224) and 39.0% [32.2, 45.8] (78/200) of samples in each country, respectively (Figures 4C and 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with confidence intervals, shown in Figures 4C and 5C.

claim: Only one sample tested positive in the T. b. gambiense-specific assay in each country.
source: Only one sample tested positive in the T. b. gambiense-specific assay in each country (Figures 4B and 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the screening shown in Figures 4B and 5B.

claim: 23.2% [17.7, 28.7] (52/224) of the samples in Côte d'Ivoire were positive for T. congolense.
source: In total, 23.2% [17.7, 28.7] (52/224) of the samples in Côte d'Ivoire and 7.5% [3.8, 11.2] (15/200) in Guinea were positive for T. congolense.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with confidence intervals.

claim: 7.5% [3.8, 11.2] (15/200) of samples in Guinea were positive for T. congolense.
source: In total, 23.2% [17.7, 28.7] (52/224) of the samples in Côte d'Ivoire and 7.5% [3.8, 11.2] (15/200) in Guinea were positive for T. congolense.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with confidence intervals.

claim: A single sample from Côte d'Ivoire tested positive in the T. suis-specific SHERLOCK assay.
source: Additionally, a single sample from Côte d'Ivoire tested positive in the T. suis-specific SHERLOCK assay.
evidence: This is a finding from the screening.

claim: No RNA from T. vivax or T. theileri was detected with the IFX SHERLOCK assay.
source: Furthermore, no RNA from T. vivax or T. theileri was detected with the IFX SHERLOCK assay.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the screening.

claim: 15.2% [10.5, 19.9] of the samples from Côte d'Ivoire showed co-infections with a Trypanozoon species and T. congolense.
source: Overall, 15.2% [10.5, 19.9] of the samples from Côte d'Ivoire showed co-infections with a Trypanozoon species and T. congolense.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with confidence intervals.

claim: Most PCR-derived molecular techniques currently used for detecting animal trypanosomes have a detection limit of 1–10 parasites/ml using genus- or species-specific primers.
source: Most PCR-derived molecular techniques currently used for detecting animal trypanosomes have a detection limit of 1–10 parasites/ml using genus- or species-specific primers, 50 parasites/ml using pan-species ITS1 primers (Desquesnes et al., 2022a) or 5 parasites/ml using 18S rRNA-targeting primers (Deborggraeve et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Desquesnes et al., 2022a and Deborggraeve et al., 2006.

claim: Each SHERLOCK4AAT assay can be run in 2 hr 30 min at 2.5 € per test.
source: In the current version of the SHERLOCK4AAT toolbox, each assay can be run in 2 hr 30 min, in a two-step reaction, at 2.5 € (exclusive of initial sample processing) (Sima et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the practical characteristics of the assay, with citation to Sima et al., 2022.

claim: SHERLOCK4AAT was not developed for direct case diagnosis in the field, but rather for eco-epidemiological surveillance at large scale.
source: SHERLOCK4AAT was not developed for direct case diagnosis in the field, but rather for eco-epidemiological surveillance at large scale.
evidence: This is a statement about the intended use of the toolbox.

claim: T. b. gambiense infections in pigs are frequently reported in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: T. b. gambiense infections in pigs are frequently reported in sub-Saharan Africa (Ebhodaghe et al., 2018; Okello et al., 2022a) and these domestic animals likely represent an underestimated reservoir of human-infective parasites (Büscher et al., 2018; Mehlitz and Molyneux, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ebhodaghe et al., 2018 and Okello et al., 2022a.

claim: Pigs likely represent an underestimated reservoir of human-infective parasites.
source: T. b. gambiense infections in pigs are frequently reported in sub-Saharan Africa (Ebhodaghe et al., 2018; Okello et al., 2022a) and these domestic animals likely represent an underestimated reservoir of human-infective parasites (Büscher et al., 2018; Mehlitz and Molyneux, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Büscher et al., 2018 and Mehlitz and Molyneux, 2019.

claim: The use of conventional molecular diagnostics on 97 free-range pigs in Côte d'Ivoire resulted in an overall positivity rate of 57% for Trypanozoon DNA and 24% for T. congolense forest DNA.
source: The use of conventional molecular diagnostics on 97 free-range pigs resulted in an overall positivity rate of 57% for Trypanozoon DNA (PCR-TBR) and 24% for T. congolense forest DNA (PCR-TCF), with 14% of pigs positive in both PCRs and none positive for T. vivax (PCR-TVW) (N'Djetchi et al., 2017; Traoré et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to N'Djetchi et al., 2017 and Traoré et al., 2021.

claim: The prevalence of T. b. gambiense infections in the two populations of domestic pigs was 0.45 ± 0.9% in Côte d'Ivoire and 0.50 ± 1.0% in Guinea.
source: Considering the resulting low prevalence of T. b. gambiense infections in these two populations of domestic pigs (0.45 ± 0.9% in Côte d'Ivoire to 0.50 ± 1.0% in Guinea) and the short life expectancy of domestic pigs reared for commercial purposes in these two rural areas (6–8 months), these animals do not likely represent a significant risk to the elimination of gHAT.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with uncertainty estimates.

claim: Domestic pigs reared for commercial purposes in these two rural areas have a short life expectancy of 6–8 months.
source: Considering the resulting low prevalence of T. b. gambiense infections in these two populations of domestic pigs (0.45 ± 0.9% in Côte d'Ivoire to 0.50 ± 1.0% in Guinea) and the short life expectancy of domestic pigs reared for commercial purposes in these two rural areas (6–8 months), these animals do not likely represent a significant risk to the elimination of gHAT.
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about pig husbandry in these areas.

claim: These animals do not likely represent a significant risk to the elimination of gHAT.
source: Considering the resulting low prevalence of T. b. gambiense infections in these two populations of domestic pigs (0.45 ± 0.9% in Côte d'Ivoire to 0.50 ± 1.0% in Guinea) and the short life expectancy of domestic pigs reared for commercial purposes in these two rural areas (6–8 months), these animals do not likely represent a significant risk to the elimination of gHAT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low prevalence and short life expectancy data.

claim: Trypanosome nucleic acids can be detected in the skin, adipose tissue and various organs even if the blood remains negative during natural infections.
source: During natural infections, trypanosome nucleic acids can be detected in the skin, adipose tissue and various organs even if the blood remains negative (Amisigo et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amisigo et al., 2024.

claim: Trypanosome DNA persists in blood and skin even after drug treatment.
source: Trypanosome DNA also persists in blood and skin, even after drug treatment (Ekloh et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ekloh et al., 2023.

claim: The absence of point of care diagnostic tests for AAT is currently a major hurdle for its surveillance and control.
source: The absence of point of care diagnostic tests for AAT is currently a major hurdle for its surveillance and control (Desquesnes et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Desquesnes et al., 2022b.

claim: Suids and bovids are the preferred hosts for most tsetse fly species.
source: In these regions, Suids (warthogs, domestic, and bush pigs) and bovids (bushbucks and buffalos) are the preferred hosts for most tsetse fly species (Serem et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Serem et al., 2024.

claim: The GAPDH gene can be phylogenetically separated into T. suis and T. suis-like strains from other African trypanosomes.
source: The multicopy GAPDH gene was used, as it can be phylogenetically separated into T. suis and T. suis-like strains from other African trypanosomes (Rodrigues et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rodrigues et al., 2020.

claim: There are three T. theileri lineages (TthI, TthII, and TthIII).
source: A conserved region between the three T. theileri lineages (TthI, TthII, and TthIII) (Brotánková et al., 2022) was selected.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brotánková et al., 2022.

claim: The target region for T. theileri has 100% identity between the described sequences of the T. theileri lineages.
source: The target region, ranging from 1014 to 1158 bp of the 18S rRNA gene (AJ009163.1), has 100% identity between the described sequences of the T. theileri lineages, and the most closely related sequences were from T. cruzi, T. rangeli, and T. dionisii, with a 97.89% identity (query coverage = 65%).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: The most closely related sequences to the T. theileri target region were from T. cruzi, T. rangeli, and T. dionisii, with a 97.89% identity.
source: The target region, ranging from 1014 to 1158 bp of the 18S rRNA gene (AJ009163.1), has 100% identity between the described sequences of the T. theileri lineages, and the most closely related sequences were from T. cruzi, T. rangeli, and T. dionisii, with a 97.89% identity (query coverage = 65%).
evidence: This is a finding from BLAST analysis.

claim: The region from 1246 to 1346 bp of the 18S rRNA gene was selected as the targeted region for T. simiae-specific SHERLOCK assay.
source: The region from 1246 to 1346 bp of the 18S rRNA gene (AJ404608.1) was selected as the targeted region for RPA amplification of the T. simiae-specific SHERLOCK assay.
evidence: This describes the target selection for the assay design.

claim: The segment 1273–1299 bp of the 18S rRNA gene has 100% identity between the described sequences of T. simiae.
source: The segment 1273–1299 bp that corresponds to the crRNA sequence has 100% identity between the described sequences of T. simiae (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The region from 389 to 528 bp of the GAPDH gene has been selected as the targeted region for T. suis-specific SHERLOCK assay.
source: The region from 389 to 528 bp of the GAPDH gene (MK962702.1) has been selected as the targeted region for RPA amplification of the T. suis-specific SHERLOCK assay (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the target selection for the assay design, shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The T. suis target region is 100% conserved between T. suis species.
source: This region is 100% conserved between the T. suis species described, and outside this clade, the most closely related sequences were found in T. congolense, with 90% of identity (query coverage >90%).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: Outside the T. suis clade, the most closely related sequences were found in T. congolense, with 90% of identity.
source: This region is 100% conserved between the T. suis species described, and outside this clade, the most closely related sequences were found in T. congolense, with 90% of identity (query coverage >90%).
evidence: This is a finding from BLAST analysis.

claim: The T. suis crRNA target fragment can only align to T. suis sequences but not to that of other Kinetoplastea species.
source: The segment 410–437 bp of the gGAPDH gene (MK962702.1), that corresponds to the crRNA target region, is highly conserved between T. suis species, with 100% identity, and the BLAST analysis showed that this target fragment can only align to T. suis sequences but not to that of other Kinetoplastea species (taxid:5653).
evidence: This is a finding from BLAST analysis.

claim: No unspecific cross-reaction was observed with host-derived genetic material.
source: Additionally, no unspecific cross-reaction was observed with the host-derived genetic material, as assessed by testing RNA from pig blood (SHERLOCK single pan-trypanosomatid and pan-Trypanozoon assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multiplexing crRNAs increased the performance of the pan-trypanosomatid assay, especially for lower dilutions.
source: Comparative analyses between the two versions were performed and multiplexing was shown to increase the performance of the assay, especially for the lower dilutions evaluated (100, 500, and 103 p/ml) by increasing the fold-change readouts of these positive controls by 1-, 2.5-, and 3-fold-change units, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A higher concordance was observed between the results obtained with the pan-Trypanozoon SHERLOCK assay and the multiplexed pan-trypanosomatid SHERLOCK assay (25.7% of double positives) compared to the simple version (7.8% of double positives).
source: Furthermore, a higher concordance was observed between the results obtained on the same samples with the pan-Trypanozoon SHERLOCK assay and the multiplexed pan-trypanosomatid SHERLOCK assay (25.7% of double positives), as compared to the simple version (7.8% of double positives) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The TgsGP-positive sample from the district of Bonon, Côte d'Ivoire was negative for all other SHERLOCK assays and all parasitological tests.
source: The TgsGP-positive sample from the district of Bonon, Côte d'Ivoire was negative for all other SHERLOCK assays, as well as in all parasitological tests.
evidence: This is a finding from the screening results.

claim: The TgsGP-positive sample from Guinea was positive in the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid SHERLOCK assay and in the CATT and mAECT tests, but negative in the pan-Trypanozoon SHERLOCK assay.
source: In contrast, the TgsGP-positive sample from Guinea was positive in the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid SHERLOCK assay, as well as in the CATT and mAECT tests, but it was negative in the pan-Trypanozoon SHERLOCK assay.
evidence: This is a finding from the screening results.

claim: 24/219 individuals (11.0 ± 4.1%) in Côte d'Ivoire tested positive in the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid, the pan-Trypanozoon, and the T. congolense-specific assays.
source: In total, 24/219 individuals (11.0 ± 4.1%) in Côte d'Ivoire and 13/200 in Guinea (6.5 ± 3.4%) tested positive in the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid, the pan-Trypanozoon, and the T. congolense-specific assays.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with uncertainty estimates.

claim: 13/200 individuals in Guinea (6.5 ± 3.4%) tested positive in the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid, the pan-Trypanozoon, and the T. congolense-specific assays.
source: In total, 24/219 individuals (11.0 ± 4.1%) in Côte d'Ivoire and 13/200 in Guinea (6.5 ± 3.4%) tested positive in the multiplex pan-trypanosomatid, the pan-Trypanozoon, and the T. congolense-specific assays.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with uncertainty estimates.

claim: Triple positive results indicate co-infections involving both a Trypanozoon species (likely T. b. brucei) and T. congolense.
source: These triple positive results indicate co-infections involving both a Trypanozoon species (likely T. b. brucei) and T. congolense (Figures 4D and 5D).
evidence: This is an inference from the test results, shown in Figures 4D and 5D.

claim: 9/219 samples (4.1 ± 2.6%) from Côte d'Ivoire tested positive in the pan-Trypanozoon and the T. congolense assays.
source: In addition, 9/219 samples (4.1 ± 2.6%) from Côte d'Ivoire tested positive in the pan-Trypanozoon and the T. congolense assays, which also represented co-infections with T. brucei s.l. and T. congolense.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with uncertainty estimates.

claim: Samples positive in both pan-Trypanozoon and T. congolense assays represent co-infections with T. brucei s.l. and T. congolense.
source: In addition, 9/219 samples (4.1 ± 2.6%) from Côte d'Ivoire tested positive in the pan-Trypanozoon and the T. congolense assays, which also represented co-infections with T. brucei s.l. and T. congolense.
evidence: This is an inference from the test results.

claim: Samples that were positive in the pan-Trypanozoon assay but negative in the TgsGP assay were presumed to be T. b. brucei infections.
source: As there is no specific test for T. b. brucei, samples that were positive in the pan-Trypanozoon assay but negative in the TgsGP assay were presumed to be T. b. brucei infections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of a specific test and the pattern of results.

claim: The analytical sensitivities obtained by the pan-trypanosomatid, pan-Trypanozoon, T. theileri, and T. congolense SHERLOCK assays were comparable with those of other existing molecular tools.
source: Therefore, in total, the analytical sensitivities obtained by the pan-trypanosomatid, pan-Trypanozoon, T. theileri, and T. congolense SHERLOCK assays were comparable with those of other existing molecular tools.
evidence: This is a comparative inference based on the LoD data and literature.

claim: SHERLOCK detects RNAs, probing for active infections.
source: Yet, a significant difference in favour of using SHERLOCK4AAT is that it detects RNAs, probing for active infections.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the SHERLOCK assay based on its molecular target.

claim: The T. vivax SHERLOCK assay did not meet the sensitivity requirements for the molecular diagnosis of animal trypanosomes.
source: The T. vivax SHERLOCK assay, targeting the single-copy IFX gene (Autheman et al., 2021), did not meet the sensitivity requirements for the molecular diagnosis of animal trypanosomes and would require the identification of another target.
evidence: This is an evaluation of the assay performance with citation to Autheman et al., 2021.

claim: SHERLOCK can detect synthetic targets at a concentration of 2 aM in optimal conditions.
source: Both assays were able to detect 10–100 fM of the synthetic controls, far from the detection capacity of SHERLOCK, which can detect synthetic targets at a concentration of 2 aM in optimal conditions (Gootenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gootenberg et al., 2017.

claim: All SHERLOCK4AAT tests are optimized for high throughput screening with a fluorescence readout.
source: All tests are optimized for high throughput screening with a fluorescence readout; hence, they can be performed in standard lab conditions by a technician trained for basic molecular biology.
evidence: This describes the technical characteristics of the assays.

claim: The findings are consistent with the most recent known distribution of animal trypanosomes in free-ranging pigs raised in Côte d'Ivoire's historical gHAT foci.
source: These findings are consistent with the most recent known distribution of animal trypanosomes in free-ranging pigs raised in Côte d'Ivoire's historical gHAT foci.
evidence: This is a comparative inference based on the study results and previous knowledge.

claim: The epidemiological status of AAT in Guinea is unclear, as no large-scale molecular studies have been published so far.
source: The epidemiological status of AAT in Guinea is unclear, as no large-scale molecular studies have been published so far.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge regarding AAT in Guinea.

claim: The lack of samples positive for T. vivax or T. theileri confirms that pigs are not frequent carriers of these species.
source: The lack of any samples positive for T. vivax or T. theileri in any study areas confirms that pigs are not frequent carriers of these species (Fetene et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the negative results, supported by citation to Fetene et al., 2021.

claim: The blood samples positive for T. b. gambiense in each study site provide further evidence of the ability of pigs to carry human trypanosomes and to act as potential reservoirs.
source: However, the blood samples positive for T. b. gambiense in each study site provide further evidence of the ability of pigs to carry human trypanosomes and to act as potential reservoirs.
evidence: This is an inference from the positive T. b. gambiense results.

claim: The presence of T. b. gambiense genetic material in pig samples has already been suspected in Côte d'Ivoire.
source: Similarly, the presence of T. b. gambiense genetic material in pig samples has already been suspected in Côte d'Ivoire (Traoré et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Traoré et al., 2021.

claim: There may exist uncharacterized trypanosome species circulating among these reservoirs.
source: In line with this hypothesis, there may also exist uncharacterized trypanosome species circulating among these reservoirs, as described in small mammals in central and East Africa (Votýpka et al., 2022), and that were only detected by the broad multiplex pan-trypanosomatid assay.
evidence: This is speculation based on the unexplained positive results and citation to Votýpka et al., 2022.

claim: The results confirm the effectiveness of the SHERLOCK4AAT toolbox in analysing the distribution of trypanosomes in hypo-endemic gHAT foci.
source: Altogether, these results are consistent with those reported in the few available previous studies (N'Djetchi et al., 2017; Traoré et al., 2021) and confirm the effectiveness of the SHERLOCK4AAT toolbox in analysing the distribution of trypanosomes in hypo-endemic gHAT foci.
evidence: This is an inference from the consistency of results with previous studies, supported by citations to N'Djetchi et al., 2017 and Traoré et al., 2021.

claim: Applying SHERLOCK detection on skin samples would be useful for monitoring both blood and skin-dwelling parasites.
source: Hence, applying SHERLOCK detection on skin samples in the future would be useful for monitoring both blood and skin-dwelling parasites.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications.

claim: The future development of multiplexed assays combined with adapted lateral flow tests would be highly desirable for reaching field-applicable point-of-care molecular diagnostic versions.
source: The future development of multiplexed assays combined with adapted lateral flow tests would also be highly desirable for reaching field-applicable point-of-care molecular diagnostic versions of the tests useable in the field.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future development needs.

claim: Considering the low prevalence of T. b. gambiense infections and short life expectancy of pigs, these animals do not likely represent a significant risk to the elimination of gHAT, as apparently confirmed by the absence of new human cases and low abundance of tsetse flies.
source: This is apparently confirmed by the absence of new human cases as well as by the low abundance of tsetse flies in the two sites (article in preparation).
evidence: This is an inference supported by additional unpublished data.

claim: Pigs are often raised in close proximity to humans, increasing the risk of animal to human trypanosome transmission.
source: This is all the more important than pigs are often raised in close proximity to humans, increasing the risk of animal to human trypanosome transmission, reinforcing our efforts to integrate the detection of both animal and human parasites in domestic pigs in a One Health perspective (Rotureau et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rotureau et al., 2022.
